A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same three-factor estimation framework and 115-pretext-task benchmark despite the changed title. All pages were readable, including v2's supplementary sections. The reporting inconsistencies identified below are document issues, not extraction gaps.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 experiments comparing estimated performance with actual semi/self-supervised performance, including scatterplots and Pearson correlations.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, robustness experiments, and resource measurements in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The specified prototype-alignment procedure changes: v1 uses f_target to extract labeled embeddings, whereas v2 uses f_pretext for both class prototypes and unlabeled embeddings. This is a limited procedural correction; the three-factor estimator, successive filtering, and final product remain intact.

E1.justification: V2 retains CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and the same 115 augmentation-based pretext tasks, while adding ImageNet-200 and Office-31. Office-31 introduces a distinct distribution-shift scenario, using Amazon labeled data and DSLR/Webcam unlabeled data.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds an explicit resource-efficiency comparison against conventional full semi-supervised and self-supervised training plus validation. The seven named SSL algorithms in the robustness experiments supply target training outcomes rather than competing performance estimators; no alternative pretext-task selection estimator is introduced.

E3.justification: The original basic CIFAR protocol is retained. V2 adds protocols using native SSL algorithms, ResNet-50, an estimation budget of 50 unlabeled samples per labeled sample instead of 10, and separate tests with 10 epochs or a 1e-5 learning rate. It also introduces cross-domain sampling and a timed resource comparison.

E4.justification: V1 has no component ablations or systematic robustness analyses. V2 adds all individual and paired indicator combinations on CIFAR-10 in Tables 2–3, plus algorithm, backbone, distribution-shift, data-volume, and hyperparameter tests. Although the text promises CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-200 ablations, those results are absent from the supplied appendix.

E5.justification: V1 reports correlation coefficients without significance testing. V2's Hypothesis Testing section adds one-tailed correlation t-tests at alpha = 0.01, using 115 tasks, 113 degrees of freedom, and a reported critical correlation of 0.226. Neither version reports repeated-run variability or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: CIFAR-10 correlations remain 0.785/0.820 for semi/self-supervised learning. Reported CIFAR-100 correlations change from 0.717/0.724 to 0.905/0.950, but v2 Figure 3 duplicates the CIFAR-10 plot and Figure 4 has conflicting paradigm labels, limiting verification. Numerous new results include ImageNet-200 correlations of 0.675/0.678, Office-31's 0.674, ablation and robustness scores, and estimation time of 29.6 seconds versus 1547.3/1651.6 seconds for full training and validation.

T1.justification: Equation 1 changes the probabilistic factorization by retaining x in the reliability conditioning and both x and the knowledge-satisfaction events in the completeness conditioning. Optimization expressions also replace indicator-loss minima with argmin expressions using named task losses. The central three-factor error bound remains, without a new theorem or substantial proof expansion.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a three-factor explanation based on learnability, reliability, and completeness, and a low-cost estimator of downstream semi/self-supervised performance. V2 foregrounds quantitative estimation and assumptions, but retains the original theoretical unification and practical contribution.

C2.justification: V2 newly interprets synchronized semi/self-supervised outcomes as indicating limited dependence on training strategy. It attributes polarized performance to amplification of beneficial or harmful pretext-task effects during training and extends its applicability interpretation to distribution shift. These explanations are absent from v1; no substantive limitations discussion is added.

D1.justification: V2 newly identifies PyTorch/torchvision, four-A800 hardware, LAMDA-SSL and Lightly implementations, and the single-A800 convention for timing measurements. It specifies Euclidean prototype assignment more clearly, while shortening Table 1's augmentation calls. Most basic training hyperparameters were already documented in v1.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion substantially broadens from a dedicated neuro-symbolic treatment to knowledge-integrated learning and expands coverage of SSL assumptions, safety, and pretext misalignment. New references include Rigollet, Mey and Loog, Von Rueden and colleagues, and He and Li; several earlier handcrafted-pretext and shortcut references are removed. This changes research positioning beyond bibliographic maintenance.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the title, abstract, introduction, and related work, and consistently shifts terminology toward assumptions and performance estimation. It reorganizes the related-work subsections, shortens the conclusion, moves future work into the supplementary material, and introduces an Impact Statement.

P2.justification: Scatterplots are redesigned from individually labeled points to operation colors and strength-dependent opacity with legends. Table 1 becomes a compact single-column display, and new ablation tables, a cost table, and extensive supplementary figures are added. CIFAR-100 presentation moves to the appendix, but Figure 3 incorrectly repeats Figure 1 and Figure 4 contains conflicting labels.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation: Tables 2–3 test the contribution of each factor, experiments with established SSL algorithms and distribution shift test broader applicability, and Table 4 directly measures the claimed cost advantage. These gains provide substantially stronger support than v1's single-backbone, simplified-loss CIFAR experiments. Duplicated or conflicting CIFAR-100 figures, unresolved references, and missing promised ablations weaken particular results, but do not outweigh the broader validation.
